parts.label: (a)
key_concepts: power as rate of doing work
component of force in direction of motion
hints: Hint 1: Rate of doing work means power. Think about which part of force X actually pushes the disc forward along its motion - the force is angled at 30 degrees, so not all of it is in the direction of movement.
Hint 2: Find the horizontal component of the 8.9 N force using cos 30 degrees, then multiply this effective force by the speed of 0.60 m s^-1 to get power in watts.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link rate of work to power**
You know that rate of doing work is just another name for power, $P$. For a constant force moving an object at steady speed, power depends only on the force component along the direction of motion times the speed.

Step 2: **Resolve force X horizontally**
Force X is at $30^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, while the disc moves horizontally. So the useful driving component is: $$F_{horizontal} = F\cos\theta = 8.9\cos30^{\circ}$$ The vertical component pushes into the ground and does no work because there is no vertical displacement.

Step 3: **Calculate the power**
Now multiply by the speed: $$P = F_{horizontal}v = 8.9\cos30^{\circ} \times 0.60$$ $$P = 4.6\text{ W}$$ to 2 s.f. This is the rate at which force X transfers energy to the disc.

parts.label: (b)
key_concepts: resolving a force into vertical component
hints: Hint 1: Pressure on the ground is caused only by the total force pushing straight down into the ground. Think about what two things are pressing the disc down onto the ground.
Hint 2: Add together the weight of the disc, $mg$, and the vertical downward part of force X, which uses sin 30 degrees, to get the total normal force $F$ on the ground.
Hint 3: Rearrange the pressure relation to make area the subject, $A = F/p$, then substitute your total force and $p = 3500\text{ Pa}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See what creates the pressure**
Pressure is defined as normal force per unit area: $$p = \frac{F}{A}$$ Here $F$ is the total force squeezing the disc perpendicularly into the ground, and $A$ is the contact area.

Step 2: **Find the total downward force**
Two contributions press down. First, the weight of the disc: $$W = mg = 0.24 \times 9.81 = 2.35\text{ N}$$ Second, the vertical component of force X, which is angled downwards: $$F_{vertical} = F\sin\theta = 8.9\sin30^{\circ} = 4.45\text{ N}$$ So the total force on the ground is: $$F = 4.45 + 2.35 = 6.80\text{ N}$$

Step 3: **Rearrange for area and calculate**
Make $A$ the subject: $$A = \frac{F}{p}$$ Substitute $F = 6.80\text{ N}$ and $p = 3500\text{ Pa}$: $$A = \frac{6.80}{3500} = 1.9 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^2$$ This small area makes sense for a compact disc under a few newtons giving a few thousand pascals.

parts.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Weight is the Earth pulling the disc downwards. Recall that a Newton's third law pair must be equal in size, opposite in direction, and of the same type, so think what is the exact opposite of a downward pull on the disc.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply the opposite-direction rule**
Weight is a gravitational pull downwards on the disc. A Newton's third law partner is always equal and opposite, so force Y must point in the exact opposite direction to weight. That means vertically upwards.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
key_concepts: Newton's third law - forces act on different bodies
hints: Hint 1: A third law pair never acts on the same body. Since weight is the Earth pulling on the disc, think about which body must feel the reverse pull from the disc.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Swap the roles of the two bodies**
Weight is the force of the Earth on the disc. The third law partner must be the same type of interaction - gravity - but reversed: the force of the disc on the Earth. So force Y acts on the Earth itself. A common mistake is to say the ground or the disc, but the contact force from the ground is a different type (normal contact) and acts on the disc, so it cannot be the pair to weight.
